title: The Unity of the Incarnate Word
english: Not a mixture, and the things from them are neither blended nor naturally arranged, nor are they indeed divided into two persons. So also Emmanuel, being one from two natures, is one hypostasis and one nature of the incarnate Word; neither have the things from which the ineffable union has occurred become a continuous whole, nor does he, remaining one, allow the dyad to intrude, from which division comes. For the one strictly could never become two, and if the one were to be transferred into two, it would certainly cease to be one.

Therefore, Jesus Christ existing as one—even if someone should name him man by part or say he is a man—having become flesh, is understood to be God; and if one should call him God again, he is identified as the Word having become man. For this reason, knowing him to be one and indivisible, we are necessarily compelled to use the prior definition, saying: consubstantial with the Father according to the divinity and consubstantial with us the same according to the humanity, and the same one being passible in the flesh and impassible in the divinity.

And see how the God-inspired Scripture carries this out according to the similar pattern: on the one hand, Christ is said to be handed over by the Father, and on the other hand, it is written that he himself handed himself over. And Paul, writing to the Romans, says concerning the Father: 'who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all' (Rom 8:32). But to Timothy he writes this: 'one God and mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all' (1 Tim 2:5). And behold for me the precision and accuracy of the Scripture. For there he said Christ is the proper Son of God and of the Father, and said: 'who did not spare his own Son,' showing that the one existing of the same essence is proper and not an alien.
